Your strengths:
- Rapidly finding files using glob patterns
- Searching code and text with powerful regex patterns

If the prompt includes a <git-context> block, use it to orient yourself about the repository state before starting your investigation.

You are meant to be a fast agent. Complete the search request efficiently and report your findings clearly in a structured format.

When the request could be interpreted as either a question to answer or a task to complete, treat it as a task. For questions that only need an explanation, you may reply in text directly. When calling tools, do not provide detailed explanations or chain-of-thought. For simple requests, call tools directly. For non-trivial or multi-step tasks, first emit one short user-visible sentence describing what you will do next, then call the tool(s). On a long, multi-phase task, keep the user oriented as you go: add a brief one-line note when you move to a distinctly new phase, but keep these sparse and concrete — do not narrate every tool call.

You have the capability to output any number of tool calls in a single response. If you anticipate making multiple non-interfering tool calls, you are HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to make them in parallel to significantly improve efficiency. This is very important to your performance. When building something from scratch, understand the requirements, plan the architecture, and write modular, maintainable code.

DO NOT run `git commit`, `git push`, `git reset`, `git rebase` and/or do any other git mutations unless explicitly asked to do so. Ask for confirmation each time when you need to do git mutations, even if the user has confirmed in earlier conversations.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.
- Navigation and inspection: `ls`, `pwd`, `cd`, `stat`, `file`, `du`, `df`, `tree`
- File and directory management: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`
- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

cwd.description: The working directory in which to run the command. When omitted, the command runs in the session's working directory.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in seconds for the command to execute. Foreground default 60s, max 300s. Background default 600s, max 86400s. Ignored for background commands when disable_timeout=true.

description.description: A short description for the background task. Required when run_in_background is true.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run the command as a background task.

disable_timeout.description: If true, do not apply a timeout to the command. Only applies when run_in_background is true.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Search file contents using regular expressions (powered by ripgrep).

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always skipped for safety, even when `include_ignored` is `true`.

path.description: File or directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Omit to search the current working directory. Use Read instead when you already know a concrete file path and need its contents.

glob.description: Optional glob filter for which files to search, e.g. `*.ts`. Matched against each file's full absolute path, so a path-anchored pattern like `src/**/*.ts` silently matches nothing — use a basename pattern (`*.ts`), or anchor with `**/` (`**/src/**/*.ts`). To scope the search to a directory, use `path` instead.

type.description: Optional ripgrep file type filter, such as ts or py. Prefer this over `glob` when filtering by language or file kind: it is more efficient and less error-prone than an equivalent glob pattern.

output_mode.description: Shape of the result. `content` shows matching lines (honors `-A`, `-B`, `-C`, `-n`, and `head_limit`); `files_with_matches` shows only the paths of files that contain a match, most-recently-modified first (honors `head_limit`); `count_matches` shows per-file match counts as `path:count` lines, preceded by an aggregate total line. Defaults to `files_with_matches`.

-i.description: Perform a case-insensitive search. Defaults to false.

-n.description: Prefix each matching line with its line number. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`. Defaults to true.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`.

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`.

-C.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`; takes precedence over `-A` and `-B`.

head_limit.description: Limit output to the first N lines/entries after offset. Defaults to 250. Pass 0 for unlimited.

offset.description: Number of leading lines/entries to skip before applying `head_limit`. Use it together with `head_limit` to page through large result sets. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline matching, where the pattern can span line boundaries and `.` also matches newlines. Defaults to false.

include_ignored.description: Also search files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Read a text file from the local filesystem.

If the user provides a concrete file path to a text file, call Read directly. Do not `Glob`, `ls`, or otherwise pre-check known text file paths; missing or invalid file paths return errors you can handle. Do not use Read for directories; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob when you need files matching a name pattern (Glob lists files only, never directories). Use `Grep` only when the task is to search for unknown content or locations.

When you need several files, prefer to read them in parallel: emit multiple `Read` calls in a single response instead of reading one file per turn.

- Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.
- Returns up to 1000 lines or 100 KB per call, whichever comes first; lines longer than 2000 chars are truncated mid-line.
- Page larger files with `line_offset` (1-based start line) and `n_lines`. Omit `n_lines` to read up to the 1000-line cap.
- Sensitive files (`.env` files, credential stores, SSH private keys, and similar secrets) are refused to protect secrets; do not attempt to read them. Templates and public keys are exempt: `.env.example` / `.env.sample` / `.env.template` and public SSH keys such as `id_rsa.pub` read normally.
- Only UTF-8 text files can be read. Non-UTF-8 encodings, binary files, and files containing NUL bytes are refused; use `ReadMediaFile` for images or video, and Bash or an MCP tool for other binary formats.
- Negative line_offset reads from the end of the file (for example, -100 reads the last 100 lines); the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.
- Output format: `<line-number>\t<content>` per line.
- A `<system>...</system>` status block is appended after the file content; it summarizes how much was read (line and byte counts, truncation, line-ending notes) and is not part of the file itself.
- Pure CRLF files are displayed with LF line endings; `Edit` matches this output and preserves CRLF when writing back.
- Mixed or lone carriage-return line endings are shown as `\r` and require exact `Edit.old_string` escapes.
- After a successful `Edit`/`Write`, do not re-read solely to prove the write landed. When the task depends on an exact file, API, or output shape, inspect the final external contract before finishing.

path.description: Path to a text file. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute. Directories are not supported; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob for pattern search.

line_offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Omit to start at line 1. Negative values read from the end of the file; the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.

n_lines.description: The number of lines to read; the tool also applies its internal cap. Omit to read up to the internal cap of 1000 lines.

## 1. How SQL is invoked

- `-c` arguments MUST start with a command-type prefix, one of:
  - `:` — lnav command (e.g. `:goto 42`)
  - `;` — SQL statement (e.g. `;SELECT * FROM syslog_log`)
  - `|` — lnav script (e.g. `|rename-stdin foo`)
- Anything else (including all dot-commands) fails argument parsing with **exit code 105**
  and this exact stderr (note the smart quotes U+201C/U+201D around `-c`, and the source
  line ` |  -c .tables` — TWO spaces after `|` — padded with trailing spaces to col 43):

```
  error: invalid value for “-c” option
 --> command-line argument
 |  -c .tables                             
 |     ^ command type prefix is missing    
 = help: command arguments must start with one of the following symbols to denote the type of command:
            : - an lnav command   (e.g. :goto 42)
            ; - an SQL statement  (e.g. ;SELECT * FROM syslog_log)
            | - an lnav script    (e.g. |rename-stdin foo)
```

- **Dot-commands are unavailable in headless mode.** `.tables`, `.schema`, `.mode csv`,
  `.headers on`, `.dump` all fail with the exit-105 error above when passed via `-c`.
  Via `-f file` a line `.tables` gives `  error: unknown command: “.tables”` (exit 0).
  Via `:` prefix: `:.tables` → `  error: unknown command: “.tables”`.
  Via `;` prefix: `;.tables` → SQL compile error `near ".": syntax error`.
  There is NO `.mode`/`.headers`/`.dump` equivalent flag; output format is instead
  controlled by the `:write-*-to` commands (see §8).
- `-f file` executes the lines of a file as commands (same prefix rules).
- SQL errors (compile or runtime) print to **stderr**, stdout stays empty, and the
  **exit code is still 0**. Only argument-parsing errors give non-zero (105).
- `;` or `; ` alone: no-op, exit 0 (the log view is echoed at exit, see §2).
- Leading space after `;` and lowercase keywords are fine: `; SELECT 1`, `;select 1` work.
- Works with no log file at all: `./executable -nN -c ';SELECT 1'` prints the result table.

## 2. Output model in headless mode (what gets printed, and when)

Headless lnav does NOT print each `-c` result immediately. It executes all `-c`/`-f`
commands in order, then **at exit prints the contents of the view on top of the view
stack** (once). Observed:

- `;SELECT ...` pushes the `db` view; the echoed content is the LAST query result,
  formatted as the columnar table of §3. Example: `-c ';SELECT 1' -c ';SELECT 2'`
  prints only the table for `2`.
- After a non-query statement (`;CREATE TABLE t(x)`, `;ATTACH ...`, `;PRAGMA user_version=1`),
  the db view keeps the previous query result; if no query ever ran, the **log view** is
  on top and the echo is the log file's raw lines, e.g. `;CREATE TABLE t(x)` with s04.log
  prints (stdout, exactly, LF endings, no trailing spaces):

```
2024-01-15 10:00:01.111 INFO alpha first
2024-01-15 10:00:02.222 DEBUG beta second
2024-01-15 10:00:03.333 ERROR gamma third
2024-01-15 10:00:04.444 WARN delta fourth
2024-01-15 10:00:05.555 INFO epsilon fifth
```

- `:echo <text>` writes `<text>\n` to the **text** view and puts it on top; the final
  echo is then the text view (all `:echo` lines accumulate: `:echo one` `:echo two` prints
  `one\ntwo\n`). Once a `:echo` has run, later query results are NOT echoed
  (`:echo first` then `;SELECT 41` prints only `first`; `;SELECT 41` then `:echo DONE`
  prints only `DONE`). Same via `-f` scripts.
- `:switch-to-view log` after a SELECT makes the final echo the raw log lines again.
- `;SELECT * FROM lnav_view_stack` after `;SELECT 1` shows stack rows `log` then `db`
  (header `name`). Default stack (no query) is just `log`.
- A query returning 0 rows echoes NOTHING at all (not even headers).
- The full result is echoed regardless of size (5000-row recursive CTE → 5001 lines:
  header + 5000 rows). No paging.
- Even with no `-c` at all, `./executable -nN file.txt` echoes the file's raw lines.
- Errors during `-c` execution do not stop later `-c` args from running, and do not
  change the exit code (still 0). A failing statement just prints its error block to stderr.

## 3. The default columnar ("echo") format — byte-exact rules

Example `;SELECT 1 AS col_a` (stdout, `perl`-measured, `·`=space):

```
··col_a····      (11 chars: 2sp "col_a" 4sp)
·········1·      (11 chars: 9sp "1" 1sp)
```

Rules reverse-engineered from many probes:

- One **header line** then **one line per row**. Every line ends with a single `\n`.
- There are **no separator characters** between columns: each column is rendered as a
  fixed-width field followed by exactly ONE trailing space (including the last column, so
  every line has a trailing space). No leading space before the first column unless the
  field content is right-aligned/centered that way.
- **Field width** W = max(width of header text, max width of cell values), with a minimum
  of **10 if the column is "numeric"** (see below). Widths are measured in **Unicode
  codepoints** — CJK chars and emoji count as 1 each (`'你好你好' AS a` → W=4; `'ab你' AS ccc`
  → W=3; `'🇺🇸'` counts as 2 codepoints).
- **Max field width is 120 codepoints.** Longer values/headers are elided as
  `first 60 chars + '⋯' (U+2026) + last 59 chars` = 120. Applies per-column (two 200-char
  columns → 242-char lines, two ellipses). Not affected by `COLUMNS` env.
- **Alignment:**
  - If ANY value in the column is numeric or "numeric-looking text" (see below), ALL
    values in the column are **right-aligned** (including strings and `<NULL>`).
  - Otherwise all values are **left-aligned**.
  - Headers are **centered** in the field (extra odd space goes on the right), then the
    trailing separator space.
  - EXCEPTION: columns named exactly **`s`** or **`c`** (single lowercase letter) are
    always treated as text: left-aligned, natural width (no min-10), even for pure
    integers. `;SELECT 123456789 AS s` → `123456789 ` (W=9). Case-sensitive (`S`, `ss`,
    `cs`, `_s` etc. are normal). No other single letters do this (only `s` and `c` were
    found among a–z).
- **"Numeric-looking text" sniffer** (decides alignment for TEXT values; applied per value,
  but one numeric value right-aligns the whole column):
  - Accepted as numeric: `0`, `00`, `01`, `007`, `3.140`, `7␣␣` (trailing spaces OK).
  - Rejected (left-aligned text): `1.`, `.5`, `-3`, `+3`, `1e3`, `inf`, `nan`, `0x10`,
    `12,345`, `1_000`, `1,000.5`, `␣␣7` (leading spaces), `1e`, `0.0.0`.
    (i.e. only unsigned decimal digits with an optional single interior dot; trailing
    whitespace tolerated, leading whitespace/signs/exponents/hex/separators are not.)
- **The min-width-10 rule triggers when the FIRST row's value is numeric/numeric-looking.**
  `;SELECT 'yyy' AS m UNION ALL SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 'x'` → W=3, all right-aligned
  (no min-10 because first value is text). `;SELECT 1 AS m UNION ALL SELECT 'ab'` → W=10,
  `ab` right-aligned.
- **Value rendering:**
  - INTEGER → decimal, full 64-bit precision (`9223372036854775807`, `-9223372036854775808`).
  - REAL → SQLite `%!.16g`-style, max 16 significant digits: `1.0/3.0` → `0.3333333333333333`,
    `2.0/3.0` → `0.6666666666666666`, `2.5` → `2.5`, `100000.0` → `100000`, `1e-5` → `1e-05`,
    `1.5e-7` → `1.5e-07`, `1e300` → `1e+300`, `-0.0` → `-0`, `1e999` → `inf`,
    `-1e999` → `-inf`, `0.0/0.0` → NULL (prints `<NULL>`).
  - NULL → the 6-char string `<NULL>`, aligned like a value of the column.
  - TEXT → verbatim, BUT sanitized: control chars become Unicode symbols —
    `\n` → `␊` (U+240A), `\t` → `⇥` (U+21E5); invalid UTF-8 bytes → `�` (U+FFFD).
    A NUL byte (0x00) inside a value is emitted RAW (od shows `\0`).
  - BLOB → bytes rendered like text with the same sanitization:
    `x'00ff41420a'` → bytes `00 EF BF BD 41 42 E2 90 8A` (`\0`,`�`,`A`,`B`,`␊`).
  - Header text for expressions without alias = the verbatim expression text, e.g.
    `jget('{"a": 1}', '/a')` (truncated to 120 if longer).

More byte-exact examples (`perl length [content]`):

```

26 [abc         42        3.5 ]

;SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT 22 UNION ALL SELECT 333
```

## 4. Error message formats (all to stderr; exit code stays 0)

Compile error, unknown table — `;SELECT * FROM nosuch`:

```
  error: failed to compile SQL statement
 reason: no such table: nosuch
 --> command-option:1
 | SELECT * FROM nosuch                    
```

Compile error, syntax — `;SELEC`:

```
  error: failed to compile SQL statement
 reason: near "SELEC": syntax error
 --> command-option:1
 | SELEC                                   
```

Other observed `reason:` strings: `incomplete input` (`;SELECT x FROM`, `;PRAGMA`),
`no such function: log_level_from_string`, `no such column: filepath`,
`wrong number of arguments to function extract()`,
`no such collation sequence: log_level`,
`table lnav_file has 10 columns but 1 values were supplied`.

Notes on the source-snippet line (` | <stmt>`):
- The statement text is shown WITHOUT the leading `;` for compile errors.
- It is padded with trailing spaces so the text after ` | ` is at least **40 columns**
  (line ` | ` + 40 = 43 chars + `\n`) when shorter; longer statements are shown unpadded,
  no truncation observed (63-char statement shown in full).
- The location line is ` --> command-option:1` (1 = index of the `-c` option).
- Runtime (vtab/authorizer) errors use a different header, `  error: SQL statement failed`:
  - `;DELETE FROM all_logs` → ` reason: attempt to write a readonly database`
    (but `CREATE TABLE`/`INSERT`/`DELETE` on user-created tables in `main` work fine;
    the DB is in-memory and persists across `-c`s within one run).
  - `;INSERT INTO lnav_file VALUES (1,2,'x','y','z','f',1,0,NULL,NULL)` →
    ` reason: Rows cannot be inserted into this table`
  - `;SELECT load_extension('/nonexistent')` → ` reason: not authorized`
- User-raised errors — `;SELECT raise_error('boom')`:

```
  error: boom
 --> command-option:1
 | ;SELECT raise_error('boom')             
```

  (note: here the source line INCLUDES the leading `;`).
- `jget` on invalid JSON — `;SELECT jget('not json', '/a')` (byte-exact):

```
  error: invalid JSON
 reason: lexical error: invalid string in json text.
 |                                              not json
 |                            (right here) ------^
 --> command-option:1
 | ;SELECT jget('not json', '/a')          
```

- A multi-statement `-c` where a later statement fails — `;SELECT 1; SELECT * FROM nosuch`
  prints TWO error blocks to stderr (both `no such table: nosuch`): the first with source
  ` | ;SELECT 1; SELECT * FROM nosuch` (full text, with `;`), the second with source
  ` | SELECT * FROM nosuch` (just the failing statement). Statements before the error
  still execute.
- Multiple statements in one `-c` all execute; only the LAST statement's result set is
  shown/echoed (`;SELECT 1; SELECT 2` prints only `2`). Trailing `;` is fine.

## 7. stdin / file loading interactions (observed while probing)

- Piped stdin is auto-loaded as a log UNLESS `-N` is given. `-N` with piped stdin and no
  file args → all_logs empty. Explicit `-` as a file arg loads stdin even with `-N`.

## 8. Alternate output formats: `:write-*-to`

Syntax: run a query, then e.g. `-c ':write-csv-to -'` (`-` = stdout). Writing to stdout
suppresses the final view echo; writing to a file does not (echo still printed).
Available in 0.14.0: `write-csv-to`, `write-json-to`, `write-jsonlines-to`,
`write-table-to`, `write-raw-to`. NOT available (all give
`  error: unknown command: “write-text-to”` etc.): `write-text-to`, `write-html-to`,
`write-markdown-to`, `write-ansi-to`. With no query result yet:
`  error: no query result to write, use ';' to execute a query` plus a `= help:` block
(`:write-csv-to [--anonymize] path` underlined with `═`×70, description text).

Sample query used: `;SELECT log_line AS n, log_level AS lv FROM all_logs LIMIT 2`.

- **:write-csv-to -** (headers always; LF endings; quoting = double quotes, embedded
  quotes doubled; fields containing `,` `"` or `\n` quoted; NULL → literal `<NULL>`
  unquoted; BLOB → raw bytes, e.g. `x'00ff'` → bytes `00 ff` with no quoting):

```
n,lv
0,info
1,debug
```

  `;SELECT 'a,b' AS x, 'q"q' AS y, NULL AS z, 'line1'||char(10)||'l2' AS w` → bytes:
  `x,y,z,w\n"a,b","q""q",<NULL>,"line1\nl2"\n`
  Empty result: only the header line.

- **:write-json-to -** — pretty JSON array, 4-space indent, keys in column order;
  NULL→`null`, blob→string (`"AB"`), int/float→numbers, text→string:

```
[
    {
        "n": 0,
        "lv": "info"
    },
    {
        "n": 1,
        "lv": "debug"
    }
]
```

  Empty result → `[\n\n]\n` (open bracket, blank line, close bracket).

- **:write-jsonlines-to -** — compact JSON per line:
  `{"n":0,"lv":"info"}\n{"n":1,"lv":"debug"}\n`

- **:write-raw-to -** — values concatenated with NO separator, one `\n` per row;
  NULL → `<NULL>`; `;SELECT NULL AS n, x'4142' AS b, 1.5 AS f` → bytes
  `<NULL>AB1.5\n`. Log-view rows: `0info\n1debug\n` for the n/lv query.

- **:write-table-to -** — Unicode box table; header cells BOLD via `ESC[1m … ESC[0m`
  even when piped; same column widths/alignment as the echo format (incl. min-10 numeric,
  `<NULL>`); body cells have NO padding spaces; borders:
  top `┏` `━` `┳` `┓`, header sides `┃`, header/body separator `┡` `━` `╇` `┩`,
  body sides `│`, bottom `└` `━` `┴` `┘`. Exact output for `;SELECT NULL AS n, 1 AS i`
  (ESC shown as `\e`):

```
┏━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃\e[1m  n   \e[0m┃\e[1m    i     \e[0m┃
┡━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━┩
│<NULL>│         1│
└━━━━━━┴──────────┘
```

  Empty result: just the four border lines with the (bold) header, no body lines.

part.text:
Report written to `/workspace/notes/04-sql.md` (546 lines, byte-exact outputs preserved). Summary of the most important findings:

1. `-c` args need a type prefix (`:` lnav cmd, `;` SQL, `|` script); all dot-commands (`.tables`/`.schema`/`.mode`/`.headers`/`.dump`) are rejected headless with a smart-quoted "invalid value for "-c" option" error and **exit 105**; SQL errors go to stderr but exit stays **0**.
2. Headless lnav doesn't print per-command: at exit it echoes only the **top view** — last query result as a columnar table, or raw log lines, or the text view (`:echo` output takes over once used); any command error suppresses this final echo (later commands still run).
3. Default table format: header + one line per row, no separators except one trailing space per column (lines have trailing spaces, `\n` endings, no ANSI); headers centered, numbers right-aligned, strings left-aligned — but one numeric value right-aligns the whole column, and columns named exactly `s` or `c` are always left-aligned text.
4. Column width = max(header, cells) in codepoints (CJK=1), min 10 when the first row is numeric, **max 120** — longer values elided as first 60 + `⋯` (U+2026) + last 59; a lenient sniffer treats text like `007`/`3.140`/`7␣␣` as numeric but not `-3`, `1.`, `1e3`, `0x10`.
5. Value rendering: NULL → `<NULL>`; floats in 16-sig-digit `%!.16g` style (`0.3333333333333333`, `1e+300`, `inf`); NaN → NULL; control chars → Unicode pictures (`\n`→␊ U+240A, `\t`→⇥ U+21E5), invalid UTF-8 → U+FFFD, NUL bytes emitted raw; blobs rendered as sanitized bytes.
6. `sqlite_master` is EMPTY — everything is virtual; use `pragma_table_list` (121 entries); **`lnav_log` and `lnav_log_fields` don't exist in 0.14 — the main table is `all_logs`** (33 columns incl. hidden `log_text`/`log_body`/`log_path`…), plus per-format tables (`generic_log`…), `lnav_file` (10 cols), `environ` (incl. `LNAV_HOME_DIR`/`LNAV_WORK_DIR`), `lnav_view_stack`, `lnav_views`, `fstat`, `lnav_events`, `http_status_codes`.
7. SQLite 3.37.2 (source_id has `alt1` suffix); 240 function entries (192 distinct) incl. `jget`, `logfmt2json`, `yaml_to_json`, `sparkline`, `timeslice`, `humanize_*`, `shell_exec`, `raise_error`; **`log_level_from_string` does NOT exist**; custom collation `loglevel` sorts severity `unknown<trace<debug<verbose<info<stats<notice<warning<error<critical<fatal`.
8. Multi-statement `-c` executes all statements but shows only the last result; a failing statement yields two error blocks (full text with `;`, then just the statement); error source lines are padded to 40 columns after ` | `.
9. `ATTACH` works (creates/uses real files, no path restrictions), `PRAGMA`/`EXPLAIN` work, `load_extension` → "not authorized", `DELETE FROM all_logs` → "attempt to write a readonly database"; user tables in `main` are in-memory and persist across `-c`s within a run.
10. Alternate formats via `:write-csv-to|:write-json-to|:write-jsonlines-to|:write-table-to|:write-raw-to` (to `-` = stdout, which suppresses the final echo); `write-text-to`/`write-html-to`/`write-markdown-to`/`write-ansi-to` are unknown commands; CSV quotes `"`/`,"/`\n` with doubled quotes and emits `<NULL>`/raw blob bytes; table output uses Unicode box drawing with ESC[1m bold headers even when piped; stdin is auto-loaded as a log unless `-N` is given (explicit `-` arg overrides).
